## Design

### 2026-10-06 – Day 1: I Started My Research and Created My First PCB Draft!!!

**2h**

Day 1: I Started My Research and Created My First PCB Draft!!!

Today, I started working on my PCB idea: an alarm clock that runs away from you. I got this idea from a MrWhosTheBoss video in which he saw an alarm clock that ran away from you to get you up and running in the morning.

Part 1: Extensions
I decided to start by looking at what my project would consist of. Basically, it can be boiled down to 3 functions.
1) Producing an awakening obnoxious noise
2) Registering the loud noise
3) "Running" away

To take care of producing the loud noise, I decided to use a 5V Piezo Buzzer. It is quite cheap, often going for less than a buck, and is easy to control, as well as integrate into a PCB.

To detect the loud noise, I will use this sound sensor module, the KY-037 High-Sensitivity Microphone Sensor Module, which has good pricing at 2-3 dollars and very good frequency detection.

To make it run, I will use the TB6612FNG Dual Driver with N20 Micro Metal Gear Motors. The cost will be around $10 in total with tax. This is a splurge, but also the most functional part of the robot that code can't fix.

Part 2: PCB
Then, I switched over to the PCB. For the PCB, I needed:
1)  a microcontroller
2) a clock to keep track of time
3) a button for turning off the alarm
4) RESISTORS, so my PCB doesn't set off my fire alarm

![Screenshot 2026-10-06 204451](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/hackclub-half-life/sessions/wqTzuosjo4Cs9kmuI53ss6gj7yDmRmwn/433e7ec67a2a2be2528235681685da88781b9ea288265486f7e00e229c686931.png)
For the microcontroller, I went with the ATmega328P-PU, which is a simple and cheap microcontroller to integrate into the PCB. Then I realized that getting an ATmega328P-PU DIP-28 is better because it will be like a plug-in extension for my ATmega microcontroller to take in and out.

For the inner clock, I went with the CSTCE16M0V53-R0, which is a 16V Ceramic Resonator. This keeps the microcontroller aware of the time from the start of the program. It is relatively cheap and very efficient, so I will solder it directly onto my PCB.

For the button, I decided to go with a regular tactile button, and for the resistor, I will just use a regular 10 Ohms resistor.

Part 3: PCB Schematic
This is the section that took me the longest. I had to watch over 3 videos on how to use online PCB schematic software before finally deciding on EasyEDA.

I watched my first video on how to use the interface. In it, I learned about the parts and libraries, along with the LCSC parts ordering partnership. Then, I started working on my design, and this is about as far as I got because I couldn't find some of the exact parts I wanted in the libraries, so I will have to make them myself.

![Screenshot 2026-10-06 203951](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/hackclub-half-life/sessions/wqTzuosjo4Cs9kmuI53ss6gj7yDmRmwn/6c960141018dfdc17daf60cf61c3610e4d9400b5a509851fc8991658fdbc2591.png)

And that's about all I got done!

Time Spent: 2 hours

### 2026-10-08 – Day 2: Finish up my PCB schematic!

**3h**

Day 2: Finish up my PCB schematic!

Today I finally finished my PCB!

![Screenshot 2026-10-08 183900](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/hackclub-half-life/sessions/wqTzuosjo4Cs9kmuI53ss6gj7yDmRmwn/b6f2aa57c013d8f72435f7360f9f08e303c693646d693c70a1d98de27e422fef.png)

This PCB is much improved from my Version 1 from yesterday. This PCB contains a microcontroller unit, sound  control (more on that later), motor control (also more on that later), and quite a few capacitors so the circuit does not fry up the second it is connected to a power source.

Part 1: Clarifications
In my Day 1 report, I should have been much more thorough about how my board will work and its connections.  Today, I will go more into the depths of the project.

Matter #1. My board is NOT optimized to solder directly to my modules, like sound and motor. I am a beginner; therefore, I do not trust myself to correctly solder the more expensive modules to a PCB and do it right. Instead, for all modules (and the Microcontroller), I will have a panel of 1 by x number of male pin connectors to hook up to the banded female wires/ribbon cables that go to corresponding male pins on these modules.

![image](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/hackclub-half-life/sessions/wqTzuosjo4Cs9kmuI53ss6gj7yDmRmwn/0f1ff76850c1002a2fbf3c3f388fefc8a8a959a819d28ebf78224b9e6f0427e1.png)

Matter #2. THE DETAILS:
Last I checked, I only outlined those parts and the basic functionality of my design. We are going to change that by showing the connections between different parts and pieces in my project. PS. I did my deep research into this stuff today, so my writing might be a bit fried

First off, the microcontroller. The microcontroller is going to serve as the main command, with almost all parts linking to it in some way or another. The ATmega328P microcontroller that I chose is a very good option because of its dirt-cheap price, along with a multitude of pins and good quality. I will not go over all of the connections to it, but I connect it to the button and resistor sequence, sound module, and motor driving units.

Next, the clock/16mHz ceramic resonator is going to be necessary for my project because it is one based on time, and this part keeps track of time. It is only connected to the microcontroller.

The button and resistor unit is there to turn off the alarm, a necessary part to ensure that I don't get worse hearing. It is only connected to the board and each other; though important to note, it is connected to the RESET pin, an important part of the build.

The sound module is the part of the build the user interacts with the most, so I splurged and went for the KY-037, which allows for more complicated algorithms to be built, like detecting different frequencies and sounds, instead of blaring at any sound it hears. It is connected to the microcontroller and the battery unit.

My motor units are actually split up into 2 sections: the driver and the output headers. The motor drivers help connect the motor to communicate with the microcontroller without frying itself. I went with the MX1508, which had MOSFETS in it to easily make efficient use of the motors. The output headers and just a screw-wire connection, so I added those in; however, I am not fully convinced about which motor output module I should use, so that will remain unknown until I figure it out.

Finally, the battery pack is going to be 4 AA batteries. This will be connected up to my screw terminal (connected to the microcontroller VCC, then that to anything that needs power) and then to my step converter, which will knock back the voltage to a manageable level of +5V. For this, I went with the LM7805 step-down converter.

![Screenshot 2026-10-08 193701](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/hackclub-half-life/sessions/wqTzuosjo4Cs9kmuI53ss6gj7yDmRmwn/4e44e75916859e4d6850b29a979ce3fb4cc053f35f23212e4c9aec28c69662d2.png)

Part 2: What I got accomplished on the PCB

So, I got lots done on the PCB. First, I found all of my parts (my sound, motor, and battery modules). This took me around an hour to scavenge for. Then, I added them in and routed everything together, which took me another hour. Clarifications for how are up above.

That's all I got accomplished today :)
